 The student financial aid office sits on the fifth floor of Aber Hall. The Trump administration introduced the Student Tuition and Transparency System and Earnings Accountability, set to begin in July 2027, which cuts off federal loans to low-earning degrees.
 Mars Johnson / Montana Kaimin 
 The One Big Beautiful Bill Act created lifetime federal loan caps for college students in July, adding complexity to the financial aid process, which many students say is already difficult. 
 The Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or FAFSA, is open, and a new lifetime federal loan cap of $257,500 affects many University of Montana students by limiting how much they can borrow before turning to private loans. 
 “This is extremely difficult because I am poor and need the money,” said Caitlin King, a 19-year-old philosophy major in the pre-law program and sophomore at the University. King is one of many students that use aid from FAFSA or other financial aid services, and the new limit caps have added another step to college planning.  
 The One Big Beautiful Bill Act went into effect on July 1 and affects loans for all years of college. This includes both undergraduate and graduate school, which leaves a difficult choice for many out-of-state students.  
 The average price for an out-of-state undergrad student to spend four years at UM is $241,816, according to the University. While this number is still under the cap, it means that many UM students will be unable to rely on loans if they want to go to graduate school after receiving their bachelor’s degree. Graduate School for an out-of-state student is $50,000, which would put students over the cap in a year if they relied on federal loans as undergrads.  
 In-state students are also impacted. The average cost for in-state students is $136,344 for all four years. Graduate school costs $34,923 per year for such students. This means that in-state students could use loans to pay for a master’s degree, which typically requires one or two years of graduate school, but a four to seven-year Ph.D. may be out of the question. This means families may have to pay out of their own pocket, but not everyone can do that. 
 “I am independent, and I had to prove it to the University last year that my parents were not able to help me,” King said. “How am I supposed to pay for my graduate school?”  
 The price of school is not the only thing affected by the cap on student loans. Paying up front for college means a student may have to take out private loans, which can require payments starting the next month.  
 “I am limited in what I can afford for housing, especially with the prices in Missoula,” King said. “If I have another payment to make, I am suddenly in an unstable environment because I can’t afford good housing, food and loans.” 
 Drew Riley, who serves as UM’s chief enrollment officer, explained that the University’s financial aid office can educate students about those loans. “So many students require loans, and we are offering a safe space for students to better understand their private loan options,” he said. These safe spaces include the Education Loan Management for an online option, but also in-person services at the financial aid office. 
 Banks and credit unions rely on credit scores to check if someone is able to pay the loan back. If a payment is missed, because the loan is through the bank, it has the ability to lower the credit score. This is one of the reasons the FAFSA was created as a way to help students directly. 
 “We are running a campaign on information, and communicating proactively with everyone, to make sure that every student is equipped with the knowledge of what the next steps for college look like,” Riley said. The University has been attempting to build a system that works with national law.  
 Lily Peterson / Montana Kaimin 
 The University started prep work for this act in the spring of 2025, and helped work with the Education Loan Management Resources. This website allows students to compare their private loan options in an easier and more seamless way. UM spent the spring and summer getting it set up as prep for the bill since no university was given the guidelines until July when the bill was put into effect.  
 The bill also limited graduate student borrowing specifically, in addition to lifetime caps. The first limit is a loan cap of $20,500 per year for graduate students, which is $14,423 less than the average cost of graduate school at the University for someone in-state.  
 Out-of-state tuition costs an average of $55,666, which means that students have to get more private loans or pay the difference out of pocket. It also caps at a limit of $100,000 for grad school, even if a student has no loan spending from undergraduate studies. Riley said that it will have effects on enrollment in the coming years, which has already taken a hit for graduate students. 
 The enrollment numbers for fall 2026 were released a few weeks ago. One takeaway is that there was a 68-person decrease, or 5%, in continuing graduate students from spring 2025 to fall 2026. However, the total number of students in graduate school did increase by 27.  The Alexander Blewitt III School of Law also saw a total decrease of six students between spring 2025 and fall 2026.  
 “We are preparing for an enrollment decline, but this bill does change the idea many graduates have from ‘How much can I borrow?’ to ‘How much should I borrow?’” Riley said. These limitations are already making their presence known to many students who are questioning if they can stay in Montana.  
 “I was planning on attending graduate school here, but with these new amounts, I should’ve just stayed in Iowa,” said Paxton Panada, an 18-year-old freshman majoring in anthropology. Panada is one out-of-state student who pays toward the maximum amount of $60,000 a year and is starting to question the next steps. 
 “I am a little bit pissed off about it, and I don’t know what else to do in my future to keep me in college, but won’t bury me under financial death,” Panada said.  
 For a lot of students, the new bill is not the first headache they have faced with financial aid, but the most recent one.  
 David Wolfe, a second-year wildlife biology major, said that the University tried to pull money from his account and didn’t notify him when it failed. The University then spent months adding interest fees for not paying the bill on time until it reached a maximum, and then sent out the notification, according to Wolfe. 
 “Suddenly the school told me I had three days to pay back all of the money, which was thousands of dollars, or I would be dropped from all my classes,” he said. The amount after the failed payment was thousands higher than it was before, which meant more money was taken out.  
 “The process to get the refund was so long, and I would not wish it upon my worst enemy,” Wolfe said. He then proceeded to take out several private loans and was in the negative for all of his bank accounts for months until the University announced a refund on the extra thousands of dollars.  
 “I hope that it doesn’t happen to anyone, because no one deserves to live in the negative, or be without a degree because the government doesn’t want to help the people that need help,” Wolfe said.
